Respirometry trials conducted on adult Large-eared tenrecs (Geogale aurita) under controlled thermal conditions revealed a maximum basal metabolic rate of 7.73 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 7.73 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at an ambient temperature of 30.9 °C [T = 30.9 °C]. This modest metabolic output, typical of small-bodied afrotherian mammals that employ heterothermy as an energy conservation strategy, reflects the species' insectivorous diet and seasonally unpredictable resource environment in the dry forests and littoral woodlands of eastern and northern Madagascar. The energetic cost of maintaining homeostasis at thermoneutrality in this diminutive tenrec is thus remarkably low, a trait that likely facilitates survival during extended periods of food scarcity or torpor.

Neonatal Large-eared tenrecs are among the smallest of any Afrotheria, with newborns weighing approximately 0.7 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.7 grams] based on measurements from captive breeding colonies. This initial mass, which can vary between 0.5 and 0.8 grams in field-caught litters, underscores the highly altricial state of the pups at parturition, which are born hairless, with closed eyes, and entirely dependent on maternal care. The remarkably low birth weight is consistent with the reproductive strategy observed in other members of the family Tenrecidae, where large litters of tiny, poorly developed neonates are common.

Under stable laboratory conditions maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a comprehensive profile of the species' reproductive and developmental life-history has been assembled. Gestation lasts for approximately 59 days [tg = approximately 59 days], a duration that falls within the 54 to 69 day range noted in earlier studies of the species and which is relatively prolonged for such at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]a small mammal. The onset of reproductive maturity occurs rapidly; females reach puberty at 37 days from birth [tp = 37 days from birth], with the reported window for this developmental milestone spanning 35 to 40 days in the available literature at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C].

Continuing within the same controlled thermal environment of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the developmental trajectory of the offspring after parturition is tightly constrained. The time from birth to weaning is 27 days from birth [tx = 27 days from birth], although previously published accounts, such as those in the Animal Diversity Web, have documented a broad range of 21 to 33 days for this critical nutritional transition at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. The maximum lifespan recorded for Geogale aurita under these captive conditions is 1095 days [am = 1095 days], which corresponds to more than 2.5 years, a relatively extended longevity for a mammal with a maximum adult body weight of only 8 grams [Wwi = 8 grams], which typically ranges between 5 and 8.5 grams in wild populations at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C].

Reproductive output in the Large-eared tenrec, when assessed at a constant ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], is characterized by a moderate fecundity and a compressed breeding schedule. Females give birth to litters containing 1 to 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1 to 5 pups per litter], and under these optimal captive conditions, they can produce approximately 4 litters each year [F_R_i = approximately 4 litters each year]. This yearly reproductive rhythm is notably rapid for a tenrec of this body size and likely evolved as a response to the short window of resource abundance in the seasonal forests of Madagascar. The combination of modest litter size and high annual frequency results in a substantial potential for population turnover in favorable years.
